extracted.intended_audience: USPTO-registered patent practitioners, patent attorneys/agents, OED staff and adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings to evaluate practitioner misconduct (e.g., misappropriation of client funds, dishonesty, neglect) and to determine appropriate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(3) - Misappropriation of or failure to timely remit client funds
rubrics_metrics.description: "Misappropriation of, or failure to properly or timely remit, funds received by a practitioner or the practitioner's firm from a client to pay a fee which the client is required by law to pay to the Office" (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violation shown where practitioner received prepaid client fees and failed to remit them to the USPTO (e.g., repeatedly presenting a debit card that was declined). Case examples: Moatz v. Rosenberg (D2006-07). ALJ may require objective corroboration (bank records); practitioner should have attempted alternative payment methods (e.g., mailing a check). The record's uncontroverted evidence of failure to remit supports a finding under § 10.23(c)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) - Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not "engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation." (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO looks to common meanings (dictionary definitions) and case law to identify dishonesty/deceit. Examples constituting violations include: depositing checks on insufficient funds, repeatedly presenting payment forms known or reasonably expected to be unprocessable, and making false or misleading assertions to clients (affirmative misstatements or concealment/non-disclosure). Case examples: In re King (D2015-29), In re Diaz (D2008-10), In re Lane (D2013-07). Practitioner's failure to correct a known payment problem and affirmative misrepresentations about an application's status support a finding under § 10.23(b)(4).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) - Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes conduct that is "prejudicial to the administration of justice." (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5); 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct is prejudicial when it negatively impacts public perception or efficacy of the legal system or the profession. Examples include: failing to inform clients of Notices to File Missing Parts, non-final Office actions, or Notices of Abandonment; issuing checks/electronic payments on insufficient funds and failing to make good; and failing to cooperate with disciplinary investigations. Case examples: In re Ivey (D2013-22), In re Kang (D2012-21), Attorney Grievance Comm'n v. Rose, Bender v. Dudas. Failure to respond to RFIs or providing evasive answers that hinder investigation can itself be prejudicial to the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) - Neglect of a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not "neglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner." (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect includes failing to timely reply to Office communications (e.g., Notices to File Missing Parts), failing to remit fees causing abandonment, and failing to notify the client of the status. Neglect may be established by a single incident. Case examples and authorities: Bender (allowing abandonment by failing to inform client), Barndt (failure to pay fees leading to abandonment), Oberding (single-incident neglect), Moatz, In re Shippey. Practitioner has duty under 37 C.F.R. § 1.111 to continue prosecution and respond to Office actions; experienced practitioners "knew or should have known" consequences of failing to pay or respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.76 / Canon 6 - Competent representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Canon 6 (37 C.F.R. § 10.76) requires practitioners to represent clients competently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence encompasses timely prosecution, maintaining required funds, responding to Office communications, and informing clients of critical status developments. Failure to act competently (e.g., not keeping client informed, not timely remitting prepaid fees, allowing abandonment) breaches duties owed to client and profession and supports disciplinary findings under related regulations (§§ 10.21, 10.76, 10.83).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) - Disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibition against engaging in "disreputable or gross misconduct." (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations do not precisely define 'disreputable' or 'gross' misconduct; courts have interpreted disreputable conduct to include unprofessional conduct violative of ordinary professional obligations and honor (Poole v. United States). Violation of specific disciplinary rules (e.g., §§ 10.23(b)(4), 10.23(c)(3)) necessarily constitutes disreputable conduct under § 10.23(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate critical updates to client (notice of nonpayment/abandonment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must inform client of critical USPTO notices (e.g., Notices to File Missing Parts, Notices of Abandonment) and of failures to remit fees that affect prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely notification gives client opportunity to act to avoid abandonment or extra fees. Failure to notify—even if practitioner attempted to manage issue internally—deprives client of choices and may constitute neglect, misrepresentation (by omission), and conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice. Documentary evidence (emails, admissions) showing long delays in informing client supports disciplinary findings and potential restitution for additional revival fees incurred by client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to cooperate with OED investigations and provide requested records
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must cooperate with Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) investigations by providing timely, complete, and truthful responses to Requests for Information (RFIs) and discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond, evasive answers, refusal to provide bank or account information, or misidentification of financial institutions wastes agency resources, hinders investigations, and is an aggravating factor in sanctions. Case references: Rose; Bender v. Dudas (evasive RFI responses prejudicial). ALJ may order subpoenas where practitioner refuses to provide records; noncooperation supports harsher sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining suspension or exclusion, the presiding officer must consider four factors: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors. (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(1)-(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: ALJ should weigh evidence on duty breached (competence, candor, safekeeping of funds), practitioner state of mind (intent/knowledge/negligence), actual injury (e.g., abandonment, additional revival fees, financial harm to client), and aggravators/mitigators (lack of cooperation, lack of remorse, any offered explanations and supporting evidence). Courts treat intentionality and actual injury as supporting more severe sanctions; failure to cooperate is a significant aggravating factor. Restitution may be ordered where fees/costs were incurred due to misconduct.
